Watchlists and price alerts

A watchlist holds research candidates without pretending you own them. Alerts nudge you when price crosses a level you chose. Neither places broker orders — they support attention, not autopilot trading.

Build a watchlist with intent

Add symbols from search or a profile page. Keep the list short enough that you will actually review it.

Watchlist quotes can refresh with market data even when you have no position — useful for patience before buying.

Jump into charts and profiles

Open a chart or profile from a watched name to inspect structure and filings-linked context before you size a trade.

If you buy later, the watchlist item does not replace entering the trade in your portfolio book.

Setting alerts

Create a price alert for a level that matters to your plan — not every tick. Delivery depends on notification setup and plan limits.

Alerts can fail when devices sleep, browsers block notifications, or data is delayed. They are helpers, not guaranteed fills.

Limits and healthy expectations

Free and Paid plans may cap how many alerts you keep. Quotes may be delayed.

Use alerts to remember homework, not to outsource judgment.

This guide is educational and describes how PSX Tracker works. It is not investment, tax or legal advice. Confirm rules and figures with your broker, FBR guidance and professional advisors.

A watchlist is a research queue

The list is names you might study or already follow, not names you own. Keeping them out of the holdings list protects your performance figures from imaginary positions. If you want to remember a price you noticed, the watchlist is the right drawer. The holdings drawer is only for shares that settled.

Group by the question you are asking. A list of “dividend names I might add” and a list of “reports due this month” will stay shorter than one list of everything you have ever typed. A long list becomes wallpaper. You stop seeing the new line.

Sectors on the list follow the names the market publishes, mapped onto a stable label so “oil and gas” does not appear as three spellings. The label is a filing aid. It is not a rating and it is not a Shariah screen.

What an alert can and cannot do

An alert watches a price you set and tells you when the published quote has crossed it, if notifications are allowed and the plan limit has room. It does not place an order. It does not know why the price moved. It does not wait for the volume you wanted or the news you have not read.

Set the level from a decision you already made: “I will re-read the filing if it trades below this” or “I will review the size if it reaches the price I said was expensive.” An alert at a random round number trains you to tap notifications and do nothing.

The condition has to be on the possible side of the current price. An “alert me when it falls below” a number that is already below the price would have fired already. The app rejects impossible directions so you do not think you are protected by an alert that can never trigger.

Limits, permissions, and missed alerts

Browser notifications need permission, and they need a browser that is willing to deliver them. A phone in focus mode will swallow the ping. Treat an alert as a convenience, not as a stop-loss that exists at the exchange. If you need an order to exist, enter it at the broker.

Free and Paid plans cap how many symbols and how many levels you can watch. The cap is printed in the product. If you need more names than the cap, you are using alerts as a second watchlist. Use the watchlist for the long list and alerts for the few prices that change an action.

A missed alert is not proof the price never traded there. Data can be delayed or absent. If the level mattered, look at the broker’s chart for that day before you assume the condition is still ahead of you.

From the list to a real holding

When you do buy, record the fill in the portfolio. The watchlist will not grow a quantity by itself, and it should not. Leaving the name on the watchlist after you own it is fine if you still want the alerts. The holding and the watch are different records.

If you sell out, decide whether the alert still means something. An old “tell me above 200” on a name you no longer own is clutter, and on a capped plan it occupies a slot you might want for a name you hold.

Delete with the same care you add. Removing a symbol from a watchlist does not sell it. Removing it from holdings does not cancel a broker order. Each list talks to a different system.

Research hygiene

Open the company page and the latest filing before you add a second alert. Two alerts on a name you cannot describe is how lists replace thinking. One sentence in your own words — what it sells, why the price level matters — is enough to keep the list honest.

Do not paste a guru’s thirty tickers in one sitting. You cannot follow thirty stories. Pick the few you will actually read this month, and let the rest wait.

Nothing on the watchlist is a recommendation from the app. You typed the symbols. The app fetched quotes and, if you asked, watched a level.

Common questions

Does an alert place an order?

No. An alert is a notification when a price condition you set is met. Trades still go through your broker.

Why might an alert not fire?

The symbol needs a usable price, the condition has to be on the correct side of the live price, and plan or data limits can apply.

Is a watchlist the same as a holding?

No. A watchlist is a research list. A holding is shares or units you recorded in a portfolio.
